doc.title: Don Albert and Herbert Hall Interview, 1978-08-03

title: Changing style between instruments; Ellington baritone models
summary: Hall says each instrument changes how you play; they listened to Harry Carney, Bigard and Hodges, and Albert says Hall sounded like Carney.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: have i have any tough songs a few stuff and alto and clarinet, did you have to change your style to shift from one to the other?
Did you play the same licks? Well, the only thing I played on baritone most of them were the solos.
Well that's what I'm talking about. Would you play the same licks on baritone that you played on clarinet more or less?
No, I wouldn't think so because it's a different field. When you pick up the instrument and you feel it, you have a tendency to play it differently.
Well the reason I was thinking about that, because it struck me in listening to Cottrell's playing, that when he played tenor it was much like he'd play...
Well some of the things you do, yeah.
So the thing about it, you realize that you can't get over those alto or baritones as fast as you can and clarinet, so you have to change your style somewhat.
Did you listen to any other baritones?
Well at that time we all were listening. Oh yeah. We all were listening to Duke Youngstown.
Connie and Bigard and Hodges and those people.

He played, he played as near as Connie as anybody ever heard in my life. Yes. Well, I've read. And he can listen to the album that we had, the rockin' and swing and the sheikin' and she, the same tonation that's the same. The same tonation, the same figures. That's rated up right there with Connie.
